title: Catatonia induced by antipsychotics in an adolescent male patient with systemic lupus erythematosus: A case report
case_prompt:
A 15-year-old boy had a one-month history of intermittent fever (37.4–38.0 °C), sore throat, and fatigue unresponsive to antipyretics and cefuroxime. Two weeks before admission, he developed nausea, vomiting, anorexia, jaundice, and dark urine. He met the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus and received intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg twice daily, which improved his fever and fatigue but only partially corrected leukopenia, anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and hyperbilirubinemia. He then had a six-minute generalized seizure with postictal unresponsiveness; EEG was normal, and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily was started.

On admission, he had nocturnal episodes of disordered speech, disorientation, inattention, auditory and visual hallucinations, and persecutory delusions, with daytime lethargy. Olanzapine 5 mg daily was initiated. Two days later, his hallucinations and delusions abated, but he began displaying intermittent abnormal movements: repetitive buttock elevation with sustained posturing, maintenance of passive limb positions, echolalia, mutism, fixed staring, resistance to passive movement, and minimal responses to pain or verbal stimuli.

Initial labs showed leukopenia, anemia, elevated transaminases, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated C-reactive protein, hypocomplementemia (C3 and C4), ANA 1:1280, and anti-dsDNA antibodies 311 IU/mL; abdominal ultrasound revealed mild splenomegaly. During hospitalization, anti-dsDNA titers fell to 105 IU/mL, ANA to 1:160, and complement levels normalized. Tests for antiphospholipid, anti-NMDA receptor, anti-GABA, and anti-VGKC antibodies were negative. CSF examination was normal. Brain MRI showed slight widening of the sulci and fissures.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. NPSLE catatonia considered — “The patient in our case tested negative for all except ANA and anti-dsDNA Abs, and no notable abnormalities were observed on head magnetic resonance.”  
2. Catatonia as part of delirium considered — “From a psychiatric diagnostic perspective, if catatonia manifests later and improves sooner than delirium does, catatonia should not be discerned independently … but as a manifestation of delirium.”  
3. Antipsychotic-induced catatonia considered — “We postulate that catatonia … occurred due to the use of olanzapine, as the chronologically manifestations of catatonia developed subsequent to the use of antipsychotics, which is a recognized predisposing factor for catatonia.”  
4. Response to lorazepam and drug withdrawal supported drug-induced catatonia — “Following the discontinuation of olanzapine and the addition of lorazepam, the patient's catatonic manifestations largely subsided.”
